newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan envoy in new secret tour to UAE, Jordan.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan envoy in new secret tour to UAE, Jordan.

text.p: Taiwan's foreign minister has embarked on yet another overseas mission state media and officials said, in a trip cloaked in secrecy to evade rival China's tightening diplomatic embargo. State media said Foreign Minister John Chang had arrived in Abu Dhabi, a member of the United Arab Emirates, on Tuesday and would then travel to Jordan on Wednesday.

The Foreign Ministry, adopting the tight-lipped policy seen during previous secret sojourns by Taiwan leaders, would confirm only that Chang had left the country for "official business" but would not comment on his whereabouts.
"Minister Chang ... will be back in a few days," Vice-Minister Cheng Chien-jen told reporters. "Because of other considerations we can't provide other details before (his return)."
It would be inconvenient to name Chang's hosts, he said.
State television reported that Chang's plane was bound for Rome but that he stopped in Abu Dhabi. State radio said the United Arab Emirates and Jordan were Chang's destinations.
President Lee Teng-hui visited both in 1995.

The Liberty Times, quoting unidentified sources, said Chang left Taiwan on Monday to visit some foreign nations that have no diplomatic ties with the island but nonetheless maintain "secret and close" links. His trip could involve Europe, it added.

Chang and Vice-President Lien Chan have followed a similar pattern for numerous overseas trips in the past year, simply dropping from sight for days at a time as international and Taiwan media scurried to track them down.
Lien managed such a secret visit to Ukraine in August, triggering a minor row between Kiev and an irate Beijing. Chang angered China with visits Singapore and Malaysia in September.

Chang again slipped from sight after his December visit to South Africa, where had sought in vain to reverse Pretoria's November 27 decision to switch diplomatic recognition to Beijing from Taipei by the end of 1997.

Chang surfaced in Belgium on December 7 but failed to win access to Belgian leaders or other European or African officials there as Beijing diplomats mounted what Taiwanese officials and media said was a concerted drive to prevent such encounters.

Communist China, Taiwan's arch-rival since a civil war split them in 1949, regards the island as a rebel province ineligible for sovereign ties. It has tightened a diplomatic squeeze on Taipei in its quest to bring Taiwan under mainland rule.
Undaunted, Chang said on Monday he would visit diplomatic ally Guatemala for the December 29 signing of a peace pact between its government and leftist rebels.
The trip is one of four overseas damage-control missions planned by top Taiwan officials since South Africa, Taipei's largest ally, declared it would switch ties.
Beijing refuses ties to any country that recognises Taiwan's exiled Republic of China, but has stepped up efforts to win over South Africa and the 29 other states that still do.
